title: 倉庫の配達とパトカー  (Warehouse Delivery and Patrol Car)

segments.t: Inside a busy Sapporo warehouse, Toshi oversees a delivery with distributor Furuya while Toru Muranishi looks on. After a sharp warning about fire safety gives way to polite business thanks, Toshi and Muranishi drive off—only to spot trouble ahead. Listen to how rough warehouse talk contrasts with Muranishi's polished manners.
よろしく頼むよ。
何で業者がタバコを吸ってるんだよ。
火事になったら全部弁償させるぞ。
悪かったな、兄さん。
古谷さん、頼むよ。
いつもお世話になってます。
よく売れるわ。しばらくは稼げそうだ。
それじゃあ。
毎度。
大丈夫なんですか？あんなこと言って。
どうってことないよ。
パトカーだ！
Toshi barks out blunt orders on the warehouse floor, while Muranishi sticks to textbook business etiquette. Let's unpack their key lines.
よろしく頼むよ。
'I am counting on you.' Pairing "yoroshiku", nicely or favorably, with "tanomu", to ask a favor, is an everyday workplace way to hand off a job. Casual "yo" at the end gives it a firm, friendly push.
何で業者がタバコを吸ってるんだよ。
'Why is a contractor smoking here?' "Nande" is the punchy spoken cousin of "naze", meaning 'why'. Next comes "gyousha", contractor or vendor, and "tabako o suu", literally to inhale tobacco.
火事になったら全部弁償させるぞ。

'If a fire starts, I will make you pay for everything.' "Kaji" means a destructive fire, and "nattara" turns "naru", become, into 'if it becomes'. "Zenbu", everything, leads into "benshou saseru", forcing someone to pay compensation, capped by tough masculine "zo".
悪かったな、兄さん。

'My bad, young man.' Instead of a stiff apology, Furuya drops "warukatta na", the past form of "warui", bad—literally 'that was bad of me'. Calling Toshi "niisan", older brother, is classic street warmth toward a younger man.
いつもお世話になってます。

'Thank you as always for looking after us.' Muranishi greets Furuya with "itsumo osewa ni nattemasu", the gold-standard Japanese business greeting. "Itsumo" means always, and "osewa" means care or support.
しばらくは稼げそうだ。

'Looks like I can earn well for a while.' "Shibaraku" covers 'for a while', marked off by "wa" to set a safe horizon. Attaching "sou da" onto "kasegeru", able to earn money, expresses how things look right now.
それじゃあ。
'Well then, see you.' "Sore jaa" literally says 'well then' and doubles as an effortless casual goodbye when stepping out of a meeting. Friends often trim it even shorter to "jaa".
毎度。
'Thanks as always.' At delivery docks, drivers call out "maido", literally 'every time', as shorthand for 'thanks for your repeat business'. Two syllables do all the work of a full thank-you.
大丈夫なんですか？
'Is it really okay?' "Daijoubu" is the indispensable all-purpose word for 'okay' or 'safe'. Slipping "nan desu ka" right after it asks for reassurance when something feels risky.
パトカーだ！

'A patrol car!' Japanese blends English 'patrol car' into brisk four-beat "patokaa". Adding plain "da" turns the noun into an urgent shout from the driver's seat. Now let's listen to the whole warehouse and highway scene straight through.
よろしく頼むよ。
何で業者がタバコを吸ってるんだよ。
火事になったら全部弁償させるぞ。
悪かったな、兄さん。
古谷さん、頼むよ。
いつもお世話になってます。
よく売れるわ。しばらくは稼げそうだ。
それじゃあ。
毎度。
大丈夫なんですか？あんなこと言って。
どうってことないよ。
パトカーだ！
Keep "itsumo osewa ni nattemasu" handy for polite work greetings, and listen for "patokaa" whenever sirens appear on Japanese streets. See you in the next scene.
また会いましょう。
